# Tidy Data

## Tidy Data {.smaller}

1. Each variable must have its own column
2. Each observation must have its own row
3. Each value must have its own cell

. . .

These three rules are interrelated because it’s impossible to only satisfy two of the three

## Common ways data are "messy"

* Column headers are values, not variable names
* Multiple variables stored in one column
* Variables are stored in both rows and columns
* See the pivoting [vignette](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/pivot.html) for examples and solutions

## Why tidy? {.smaller}

A ~~biased~~ principled approach

::: {.incremental}
- There are many reasons why you might want to have "messy" data
- **But**...
- If you have a consistent data structure, it’s easier to learn tools that work with it because the data has an underlying uniformity
- There’s a specific advantage to placing variables in columns because it allows R’s vectorised nature to be optimized
- Tidy data is an **extremely** useful format generally, and particularly useful when applying tools within the `{tidyverse}`
- All packages within the `{tidyverse}` are designed to either help you get your data in a tidy format, or assume your data are already in a tidy format
- Assuming a common data format leads to **huge** jumps in efficiency, as the output from certain functions can be directly input into others

:::

## Messy data \#1

What makes this data messy? 

Or, why is this data not tidy?

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

tidyr::relig_income
```

## Messy data \#1

Column names are data (!), not variable names

There are data in the column names

```{r}
#| echo: false

tidyr::relig_income
```

## Tidy it up

We want a column for `income` level

And a column for the `count` of people at that level

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

relig_income %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -religion,
    names_to = "income",
    values_to = "count"
  )
```

## Messy data \#2

What makes this data messy? 

```{r, echo=FALSE}
(who_r <- who %>% 
  rename_with(~str_replace(., "newrel", "new_rel"), .cols = contains("rel")) %>% 
  rename_with(~str_replace(., "m", "m_"), .cols = contains("new_")) %>% 
  rename_with(~str_replace(., "f", "f_"), .cols = contains("new_")))
```

## Messy data \#2

There are many variables in column names

```{r, echo=FALSE}
who_r
```


## Messy data \#2 

There are many variables in column names

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

::: {.fragment}
Example column names
:::

::: {.fragment}
[new_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[sp_]{style='color:#009E73'}[m_]{style='color:#0072B2'}[014]{style='color:#CC79A7'}

[new_]{style='color:#D55E00'}[rel_]{style='color:#009E73'}[f_]{style='color:#0072B2'}[65]{style='color:#CC79A7'}
:::

:::

:::

::: {.fragment}

:::

::: {.fragment}

:::

::: {.fragment}
<u>and</u> these are separated by underscores `_` which is actually quite convenient
:::

:::

::::

. . .

That's a lot of information in the column names!

## Let's tidy it

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

who_r %>%
 pivot_longer(
  cols = new_sp_m_014:new_rel_f_65,
  names_to = c("diagnosis", "sex", "age_range"), 
  names_sep = "_",
  names_prefix = "new_",
  values_to = "count",
  values_drop_na = TRUE
)
```

## Messy data \#3

What makes this data messy? 

```{r}
#| echo: false

(hh <- household |> 
  bind_cols(
    tibble(
    dob_child3 = as_date(c("2001-02-19", NA, NA, NA, "2002-05-05")),
    name_child3 = c("Alice", NA, NA, NA, "Peter")
    )
    ) |> 
  select(family, name_child1, dob_child1, name_child2, dob_child2, name_child3, dob_child3))
  

```

## Messy data \#3

There are multiple observations per <u>row</u>

```{r}
#| echo: false

hh
```

. . .

We have two pieces of information (or values) for each child

- `name` and `dob` 

These need to go into separate columns 

## Tidy it up!

```{r}
#| echo: false

hh %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !family, 
    names_to = c(".value", "child"), 
    names_sep = "_", 
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
```

## Let’s look at some education data

```{r, echo=FALSE}
(exam <- read_csv(here("data", "exam1.csv")))

```

## Let's Discuss

* Are these data tidy?
* If not, what needs to happen to make them tidy?
* What are the variables? What are the values?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
(exam <- read_csv(here("data", "exam1.csv")))

```

## exam1 data

What do we want?

. . .

Let’s change all `item` variables into two variables: `item` and `score`

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
exam
```

## exam1 data

What do we want?

Let’s change all `item` variables into two variables: `item` and `score`

```{r}
#| echo: false
(exam_tidy <- exam %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("item"),
    names_to = "item",
    names_prefix = "item_",
    names_transform = list(item = as.integer),
    values_to = "score"
  ))
```

## Why are tidy data useful?

Easy to calculate the `prop`ortion of students responding correctly to each item

. . .

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| echo: false

exam_tidy %>% 
  group_by(item) %>% 
  summarize(prop = mean(score))
```

## Why are tidy data useful?

Easy to calculate the `prop`ortion correct for each item by gender

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

exam_tidy %>% 
  group_by(item, gender) %>% 
  summarize(prop = mean(score))
```

## Why are tidy data useful?

Easy to calculate the `total` and `percent` correct for each student

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

exam_tidy %>% 
  group_by(stu_name) %>% 
  summarize(
    score_total = sum(score),
    score_pct = round(score_total/n()*100)
  )

```

## Let's try another

Are these data tidy?

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

(sim <- read_csv(here("data", "longitudinal_sim.csv")))
```

## Tidy it!

We want separate columns for `wave` and `content` and `score`

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

(sim_tidy <- sim %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -1,
    names_to = c("wave", "content"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "score",
    names_prefix = "wave_"
  )
)
```


## Caveats {.smaller}

- Tidy data are excellent when conducting preliminary descriptive analyses, plotting data, linear models

- Occasionally, you need the data in a different format
    + if you're using other packages or software for analysis
    + specific modeling purposes (SEM)
    + or you have two outcomes variables that might need to be separate column
        - `math` & `rdg`

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false

sim_tidy
```

## Tidy Data Made "Simple"

1. Keep each dataset in its own tabular format
2. Put each variable in a column

## Don’t get discouraged!

It’s hard to understand tidy principles unless you spend <u>a lot</u> of time working with data

Data is often organised to make **data entry** as easy as possible

::: {.incremental}

* Tidying is tricky!
* Takes practice!
* Takes trial and error!
* Takes learning and re-learning - <u>a lot</u>!
* Takes trial and error!
* But you are ~~rarely~~ never gifted with tidy data!

:::

# Naming Stuff

## Column Naming Rules

**Do use**

- lowercase
- prefixes and suffixes!
    + `basc_score`, `basc_date`...
    + `school_name`, `school_id`, `school_location`...
- underscores "`_`"

## Column Naming

- A shortened representation of the variable
- All variable names must be unique

. . .

Column name

[prefix]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[name]{style='color:#0072B2'}

. . .

[id]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[student]{style='color:#0072B2'}
[id]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[school]{style='color:#0072B2'}
[id]{style='color:#D55E00'}_[district]{style='color:#0072B2'}

## Column Naming Rules

**Do NOT use**

- CAPS
- spaces 
- numbers to start
- special characters
    + **except** underscores "`_`"


## Data Values

- **Don't** use numbers for labels!
    + 0 == "yes"
    + 1 == "no"
    
- Just use the values!
    + "never"
    + "rarely"
    + "sometimes"
    + "often"

## Folder & File Naming Rules

**Do use**

- lowercase
- underscores "`_`" or hyphens "`-`"

## Folder & File Naming Rules

**Do NOT use**

- CAPS
- spaces!
- special characters
    + no periods, no slashes!
    + **except** underscores "`_`" or hyphens "`-`"


# Some things I liked from [these slides](https://figshare.com/articles/presentation/Data_Management_and_Data_Management_Plans/7890827?file=14698892) from Jessica Logan

## Document Everything!

- It’s so hard to remember what you measured, when you measured it, or why you measured it
- Your best strategy is organization and detail
    + well-documented protocol
    + a good codebook
    + data dictionary (documentation of what your variable names mean) 
- Future you won’t remember what current you decides to do today, or why you decided to do it
- Think about someone else using your data later, and what they will need to know

## Misc

- Back up your data
- Avoid manually-entered questions

## Let's `pivot_longer()` {visibility="hidden"}

Necessary arguments

* `data` - of course
* `cols` – which columns you will pivot longer
* `names_to` – new variable name (in quotes) for those `cols`
* `values_to` – new variable name (in quotes) for the cell values

## Let's `pivot_longer()` {visibility="hidden"}

```{r, eval=FALSE}
relig_income %>%

 )

```
